description: Bello! Gru said: "We are going to steal THE MOON!" We just want to land on it, which might be harder. At the lunar south pole the Sun barely clears the horizon and Earth vanishes for two weeks a month. Our web app uses real NASA data to show when the Sun sets and Earth disappears at any landing site, and what happens if a launch slips. Four Minions from Port Louis, crew complete. We steal the Moon. Well, we plan the landing. BANANA! Poopaye!
summary: Earth Jukebox lets people hear NASA Earth data. It turns dated NASA maps into sound and text at the same time, so blind and low-vision people can explore Earth science that is usually only shown as a picture. Each date becomes a note (higher means warmer), and the place on the map is heard from left to right. Users can play a data set date by date, explore the map by keyboard, touch or mouse, lock one spot to hear it change over time, read the same values as a data table, and download the sound as a WAV file. Learn, Compare and Ask modes help people build understanding, and an optional voice guide can explain each page. Our first real data set is 2023 sea surface temperature around Mauritius from NASA's GHRSST MUR analysis, drawn by NASA GIBS. Most Earth science is locked inside images; sonification opens it to many more people.
details:
What it does: Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns dated NASA Earth maps into sound and text at the same time. Each date in a data set plays as a note (higher pitch means warmer), and position on the map is heard from left to right through stereo panning. It has four modes. Listen plays a data set date by date in three sound styles (Simple, Full and Change from normal); users can explore the map with keyboard, touch or mouse, lock one place and hear it change across dates, read the same values as an accessible data table, and download the sound as a WAV file. Learn plays every sound once with its words. Compare asks users to listen to two dates, answer, and then see the reveal. Ask answers questions about the data from the data itself, with no server needed.

Benefits and impact: Most Earth science reaches the public as images, which leaves blind and low-vision people out. Earth Jukebox gives them an independent way to explore real NASA data, and gives sighted learners a second sense to understand patterns like warming and seasonal change. Our first real data set is 2023 sea surface temperature around Mauritius, our home island, where ocean warming directly affects coral reefs and fisheries.

Tools and languages: React, TypeScript and Vite for the app; Tone.js for sound synthesis; a small Python FastAPI server for the optional voice guide (Google Gemini Live via Google's Agent Development Kit). The app is a mobile-friendly installable web app hosted on Vercel, with unit and accessibility tests.

Creativity: Instead of a chart with alt text, the data itself becomes music. The sound mapping is deterministic, so the same picture always gives the same sound and words, and no AI model sits between the data and what you hear. Every sound has matching text, so nothing depends on hearing alone either.

Factors we considered: accessibility first (keyboard, screen readers, captions for every sound), working fully offline without the optional AI guide, honesty about limits (values are read from NASA's rendered map colours so they are approximate, and we have not yet run a test session with blind or low-vision users), and privacy (the app stores no voice or questions).
